title: ‘Wicker’ & ‘Heated Rivalry’ spark horny 4DX entertainment trend | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

In a cavernous cinema in Times Square, once famous for its seedy theaters, a crowd of people is ogling one chiseled hunk go to town on another. But these aren’t perverts; they’re “Heated Rivalry” fans. And they aren’t just watching the gay hockey drama — they’reexperiencingit. As the thrusts intensify between Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) and Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams), the theater’s seats rock back and forth with a mechanical precision that mirrors the on-screen action, culminating in fits of giggles and applause.

“Absolutely bananas,” said Alyssa Bloomberg, a 25-year-old student, after exiting the Regal Cinema for her first experience with 4DX, a technology that turns cinema seats into de facto amusement park rides. “We walked out truly having had a threesome. That was awesome.”

Others who watched the first season’s final two episodes in 4DX at a sold-out screening hoped the experience would be even bumpier. “I was expecting more movement,” said 23-year-old Leah Tejeda, “but I still felt like IwasShane.”

The popularity of 4DX cinema has been growing since itdebuted in US theatersin 2014, shaking moviegoers’ seats, while spraying them with water and wind, or dousing them with a range of smells. The technology has traditionally been associated with big-budget action films typically geared towards men, such as superhero blockbusters or war movies. In recent weeks, though, distributors and theater chains have seemingly unlockeda new genre of 4DX entertainment:4D-sex.

On the back of surprisingly popular and profitable showings of theromantasy movie “Wicker,”starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård, “Heated Rivalry” also received a much-hyped 4DX one-night-only release via Regal to celebrate the series’ one-year anniversary. (The show is streaming in the United States on HBO Max, which is owned by CNN’s parent company, Skydance.) As more women clamor to see these romances and their steamy scenes in earth-shaking 4DX, they say the experience is less about feeling titillated and more about doing something ridiculous and fun with likeminded people.

“Feeling the thrust in the sex scene was a little jarring at first, but everyone was laughing,” said Cait DeForest, a 38-year-old who works in country music media in Nashville and who saw “Wicker” in 4DX at a local Tennessee cinema earlier this month. DeForest enjoyed the experience so much she quickly paid for another ticket to catch the re-release of “Heated Rivalry” in the same format. “Going with your friends and experiencing something completely ridiculous together is fun,” she said by phone from Nashville. “Why wouldn’t we want to sit in a theater and find out what it’s like to get railed by Alexander Skarsgård or look into Shane Hollander’s yearning little bottom eyes on the big screen?”

“Wicker” is an unlikely film to have ushered in a cinematic sexual revolution. Made for just $10 million, the film is a sweet medieval fantasy in which Colman’s ostracized fisherwoman character commissions a husband to be made for her out of wicker, resulting in the statuesque Skarsgård character proceeding to rock her world and drive the other townspeople wild with jealousy. It doesn’t exactly scream “amusement park ride.”

When the distributor Black Bear Pictures acquired the movie in February after its debut at the Sundance Film Festival, the company commissioned market research to determine how best to advertise the film and to whom. “The research was like, ‘Play it safe, play it broad. Your audience is over 45,’” recalled Bianca Parkes, Black Bear’s head of marketing. That advice felt limiting, she said, and the company believed in the movie’s original premise, so they opted for a broader strategy that leaned into its relatable themes: comedy and sex.

After the film’strailerdropped in the summer, featuring a scene in which the Wicker Husband quite literally breaks the bed, online jokes about a 4DX version of the film spread quickly. “Immediately, we noticed a surge of social commentary specifically directed at 4DX. Perhaps it was initially joking, but it became obvious that it was real,” said Erik Dane, vice president of digital marketing at CJ 4DPLEX, the South Korean company behind the technology. The company posted acheeky TikTok clipacknowledging the demand that has garnered more than 2 million views — a viral response so notable it brought the two companies together to determine how to make “Wicker” in 4DX happen.

Creative technicians at the CJ 4DPLEX headquarters in Seoul began to try to determine which effects to employ at which points in the film. But working on a movie with such standout sex scenes was new for the team, who were tasked with making the love-making feel unforgettable. “Typically, they haven’t really leaned into those type of scenes in past films,” Dane said. The end result was a success. “I watched it for the first time with the filmmakers. It delivered,” said Parkes, the marketing chief.

The 4DX cut was intended as a one-night-only marketing stunt. But demand was so high for the October 28 event in 4DX cinemas across the US, that tickets sold out before they were even officially announced. A minorpressfrenzyensued — Indiewire called it“the ‘Citizen Kane’ of 4DX”— while on social media, viralrollicking videosfrommoviegoerswatching“Wicker” in 4DXhave functioned as ongoing advertisements for the movie, turning it into a weekslong affair.

Of the $23 million “Wicker” has made at the US box office, around $1.4 million of that has been via the 4DX format, according to Black Bear. “The internet really took it to this next level. Obviously, this is beyond anyone’s wildest dreams here or on the filmmakers’ side,” Parkes said. “This campaign was really very community-led and audience-led, and we’ve just played along.”

In the wake of the “Wicker” success, Regal Cinemas held a one-night-only “Heated Rivalry” event on November 16, with 96 screenings across the company’s 59 4DX cinemas. Some 10% of those sold out.

Many of those who attended the two screenings in Times Square, like 24-year-old Alyssa Napolitano, were forking out for their first-ever 4DX ticket. “I want the full lake experience with Ilya,” Napolitano said. “I want togo to the cottage, basically.”

As befitting the fanbase of the show, the crowed was heavily dominated by women and queer men, something that felt refreshing to Sarah Goldstein, 25. “You see 4DX action movies or thrillers, but women-centered media is not always as accessible to these types of experiences,” she said.

Some of the 4DX technology employed was indeed suggestive, such as the swaying — and spraying — of the chairs during an oral sex scene. But others were more immersive, such as the cool breeze that swept through the cinema when the action shifted to frosty Moscow. Bloomberg, the student, compared her immersive experience to a Disneyland ride — one that felt adult but not pornographic. “Because everyone was laughing, it felt like a beautiful moment of community and not inappropriate — even though it was incredibly inappropriate,” she said.

PJ Rosa, 32, said he had purposefully purchased only a small popcorn before the screening, worried the jostling seats would send his snacks flying. “At this point in 2026, everything is so whatever that it’s like, ‘OK, I’ll go into a room with a bunch of strangers and watch crazy gay sex,” Rosa said. “Why not!’
